paper.code_data_availability: No code or data availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project reference is given. …

registers.years: 2006 and 2010 for the regression sample; 2003-2009 for the decomposition in Fig. 1
variables_mentioned: occupation code of each employment relation
hourly wage rate of the employee

registers.role: treatment (work organization and offshoring in 2006); sampling frame for GOPA
variables_mentioned: systems for collecting proposals from employees
quality circles (formal delegation of quality control)

registers.role: treatment (work organization 2010, off-shoring 2010, innovation effort 2007-2009, impact of the 2008 financial crisis)
variables_mentioned: the same six organizational practice questions
priority to new production technology in the innovation effort (five-level Likert scale)
effect of the financial crisis on domestic sales

linkages: in the registry data each employed person is linked to at least one firm through employment relations, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate
the 2006 DISKO4 responses are linked to the 2010 GOPA responses to form a firm panel (601 firms); the sample is the overlap of the two surveys
firm-level register data (net revenue, net investments, gross profits, fixed capital stock, age, industry, region) merged onto the surveyed firms
municipality-level average real hourly wages by labour category merged onto firms as input prices

sample.universe: Danish private-sector firms responding to both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA employer surveys
sample.unit_of_observation: firm (one long difference between 2006 and 2010 per firm)
selection_rules: the DISKO4 survey resulted in a sample of 1775 employer responses
DISKO4 was used as the basic sampling frame for the GOPA survey, establishing a panel
the GOPA survey resulted in 601 firm responses constituting the panel of the two surveys
firms with less than 10 employees in either year are excluded
532 firms are available for the regressions
missing values, including 'Don't know' responses, are multiply imputed (25 imputations) rather than dropped

construction_notes: occupations classified from ISCO-88 1-digit major groups following Goos et al. (2014): high-paid/skill = managers, professionals, technicians and associate professionals; middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low-paid/skill = service workers and shop and market sales workers, elementary occupations

managers are kept separate from the rest of the high-skill group because in these data the shares for managers evolve idiosyncratically; a high-skill estimate can be obtained by adding estimates across the relevant equations
the wage level of each occupation in the data was checked to correspond to the Goos et al. (2014) hierarchy
individuals with undefined occupations are assigned their occupation in the previous or following year
employment shares and wage cost shares at a firm are obtained by aggregating all employment relations within the firm, for 2006 and for 2010
the consumer price index is used to deflate monetary values to 2006 prices

work organization is measured by two factors from a PCA of six four-category organizational-practice questions pooled over both surveys (1064 observations), built from weighted polychoric correlations; only the first factor has an eigenvalue above one (the second is 0.82) but the second is retained because the first accounts for only 52.77 percent of total variance; together they account for 66.39 percent; after oblique rotation the recalculated eigenvalues are 2.92 and 2.23 and the inter-factor correlation is 0.529
factor 1 is labelled Delegation and Integration (DI) and factor 2 Involvement (INV)

technological change is a binary variable equal to 1 if the firm both prioritized technological change in production highly or very highly and reports a great or some outcome from the innovation effort (GOPA)
the alternative technology measure is the change in the capital labor ratio, the ratio of the value of fixed real assets to full-time equivalent employment (register data)
off-shoring is measured by binary indicators of use in each year, from which indicators for having begun and for having ceased to off-shore between the surveys are constructed
input prices are the average real hourly wage for each labour category in the municipality of the firm in the relevant year; firm output is measured by sales

financial-crisis controls: dummies for some/high deterioration in domestic sales and in liquidity, and a dummy for some/high improvement in recruitment opportunities; plus the firm's 2006 gross profit margin relative to the 2006 industry average
firm age in four categories (less than five years, five-nine years, 10-19 years, more than 19 years); region = NUTS3 of the firm's main address (11 categories); size and industry each four categories
missing values multiply imputed with 25 imputations under a fully conditional specification, assuming missing at random
post-stratification weights for firm size and industry constructed from registry data
the wage of the low-skill group is the numeraire; only three of the four share equations are estimated and the fourth is derived, so the four coefficients in each row of Tables 4-7 sum to zero

claims.statement: DI (delegation and integration of functions) has no statistically significant association with the change in the firm's wage cost share of managers between 2006 and 2010 (model 1, Table 4, column Mangers).

treatment.label: DeltaDI - change 2006-2010 in the firm's score on the Delegation and Integration factor

definition.value: First factor of a principal components analysis of six organizational-practice questions (autonomous groups; systems for collecting proposals from employees; quality circles; delegation of responsibility; interdisciplinary workgroups; integration of functions), each a four-category variable (1 No/None, 2 Less than 25%, 3 25-50%, 4 over 50% of employees involved), asked identically in the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys and pooled over the resulting 1064 observations; the PCA uses weighted polychoric correlations and oblique rotation. The factor loads positively on autonomous teams, delegation of responsibility, interdisciplinary workgroups and integration of functions, and is labelled 'Delegation and Integration (DI)' in Table 2. The regressor is the firm's 2006-to-2010 long difference in this factor score; the paper notes that a unit change is very similar to a change of one standard deviation (Table 3 variance 1.156, mean of the change -0.110).

timing.value: Long difference between the 2006 DISKO4 survey and the 2010 GOPA survey, contemporaneous with the differenced outcome. The technology indicator refers to the innovation effort of 2007-2009 as reported in the 2010 survey, and the offshoring indicators to a change between the two survey years.

outcome.label: Change in the firm's wage cost share of managers, 2006-2010

register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: wage cost share (the firm's wage bill for the group divided by its total labour cost) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the managers equation of the four-equation system.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point

estimand.target_population: Danish private-sector firms with at least 10 employees in both years that responded to both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys
estimand.time_horizon: change between 2006 and 2010 (a four-year long difference)
estimand.formal_query: gamma_{j,DI} in Eq. (6): the partial derivative of the expected change in the group's wage cost share with respect to the regressor, holding the other quasi-fixed factors, output, relative wages and the controls fixed. The paper expresses it as a translog cost-function parameter, not in do-notation.

population.description: Danish private-sector firms present in both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA employer surveys (601 panel firms), excluding firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year, leaving 532 firms, linked to Danish register data on firms and working-age people
population.selection: DISKO4 produced 1775 employer responses and served as the sampling frame for GOPA, which produced 601 responses; DISKO4 oversampled firms from previous DISKO waves, so the panel is not representative of the Danish economy, and post-stratification weights for firm size and industry are used. Firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year are excluded because organizational practices require a minimum firm size to be meaningful.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-firm change between 2006 and 2010 in the quasi-fixed factors of the translog cost function - work organization (the DI and INV factors), an indicator of technological change in production, and the start or cessation of off-shoring - with firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity removed by long differencing. There is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument: the variation is the observed change in firms' own practices.

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity in the cost-minimization problem is additive and time-invariant, so that taking long differences between 2006 and 2010 removes it.

Conditional on the included regressors - the other quasi-fixed factors, the change in log sales, the changes in municipality-level relative wages, the three financial-crisis indicators, the 2006 relative gross profit margin, and region, industry and firm-age dummies - the change in the quasi-fixed factor of interest is uncorrelated with the differenced error of the share equation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing beyond the weighted correlations in Table 3; no balance table, pre-trend or placebo test is offered.

lhs: DeltaDI - change 2006-2010 in the firm's score on the Delegation and Integration factor
rhs: Delta u_j (differenced error of the share equation)

key_assumptions.assumption: The cost function is homogeneous of degree one in wages, so that a proportional increase in all wages raises total costs proportionally; the wage of the low-skill group is used as numeraire and, because the shares sum to unity, only three of the four equations are estimated and the fourth is derived.

The municipality-level average real hourly wages used as input prices are exogenous to the individual firm's occupational cost shares; the paper states the risk of endogeneity from wages entering both sides of the wage cost share equation but does not instrument it away in model 1.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Model 2 re-estimates the same specification with employment shares as the dependent variable; an alternative estimation without the right-hand side wage variables is reported in the online supplementary material and is said not to be substantially different.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.
baseline_mean is null for the wage cost share models: Table 3 reports summary statistics for the employment-share dependent variables only.

evidence.how: Table 4 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

Table 3 reports means only for the employment-share dependent variables; the corresponding correlation and summary table for the wage cost share models is in the online supplementary material, so no mean of the change in wage cost shares is printed in the paper.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

value.normalisation: The wage of the low-skill group is the numeraire, so wages enter as relative wages w_k/w_Low and only k != Low appear; the cost function is homogeneous of degree one in wages so sum_k beta_{j,k} = 0; the shares sum to unity so only J-1 = 3 of the 4 equations are estimated and the fourth (Low) is derived; the second-order Taylor polynomial is taken at the expansion point 1; firm effects are removed by long differencing 2006 to 2010; Delta ln a_{m,i} is simplified to Delta a_{m,i} because the quasi-fixed factors are mainly categorical; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices.

value.claimed_domain: Within-firm changes in Danish private-sector firms over 2006-2010. The authors claim that the organizational level is central to understanding possible trends towards job polarization, but explicitly leave it to researchers with comparable panel data for other countries to confirm the validity of the results and to assess the extent to which they apply in different national settings.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.
baseline_mean is null for the wage cost share models: Table 3 reports summary statistics for the employment-share dependent variables only.

evidence.how: Table 4 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

Table 3 reports means only for the employment-share dependent variables; the corresponding correlation and summary table for the wage cost share models is in the online supplementary material, so no mean of the change in wage cost shares is printed in the paper.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

anchor_quote.text: In terms of costs, DI substitutes for low workers while INV substitutes for middling workers.

claims.statement: DI (delegation and integration of functions) has no statistically significant association with the change in the firm's wage cost share of middling-skill occupations between 2006 and 2010 (model 1, Table 4, column Middling).

treatment.label: DeltaDI - change 2006-2010 in the firm's score on the Delegation and Integration factor

definition.value: First factor of a principal components analysis of six organizational-practice questions (autonomous groups; systems for collecting proposals from employees; quality circles; delegation of responsibility; interdisciplinary workgroups; integration of functions), each a four-category variable (1 No/None, 2 Less than 25%, 3 25-50%, 4 over 50% of employees involved), asked identically in the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys and pooled over the resulting 1064 observations; the PCA uses weighted polychoric correlations and oblique rotation. The factor loads positively on autonomous teams, delegation of responsibility, interdisciplinary workgroups and integration of functions, and is labelled 'Delegation and Integration (DI)' in Table 2. The regressor is the firm's 2006-to-2010 long difference in this factor score; the paper notes that a unit change is very similar to a change of one standard deviation (Table 3 variance 1.156, mean of the change -0.110).

timing.value: Long difference between the 2006 DISKO4 survey and the 2010 GOPA survey, contemporaneous with the differenced outcome. The technology indicator refers to the innovation effort of 2007-2009 as reported in the 2010 survey, and the offshoring indicators to a change between the two survey years.

outcome.label: Change in the firm's wage cost share of middling-skill occupations, 2006-2010

register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: wage cost share (the firm's wage bill for the group divided by its total labour cost) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the middling-skill occupations (clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers) equation of the four-equation system.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point

estimand.target_population: Danish private-sector firms with at least 10 employees in both years that responded to both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys
estimand.time_horizon: change between 2006 and 2010 (a four-year long difference)
estimand.formal_query: gamma_{j,DI} in Eq. (6): the partial derivative of the expected change in the group's wage cost share with respect to the regressor, holding the other quasi-fixed factors, output, relative wages and the controls fixed. The paper expresses it as a translog cost-function parameter, not in do-notation.

population.description: Danish private-sector firms present in both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA employer surveys (601 panel firms), excluding firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year, leaving 532 firms, linked to Danish register data on firms and working-age people
population.selection: DISKO4 produced 1775 employer responses and served as the sampling frame for GOPA, which produced 601 responses; DISKO4 oversampled firms from previous DISKO waves, so the panel is not representative of the Danish economy, and post-stratification weights for firm size and industry are used. Firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year are excluded because organizational practices require a minimum firm size to be meaningful.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-firm change between 2006 and 2010 in the quasi-fixed factors of the translog cost function - work organization (the DI and INV factors), an indicator of technological change in production, and the start or cessation of off-shoring - with firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity removed by long differencing. There is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument: the variation is the observed change in firms' own practices.

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity in the cost-minimization problem is additive and time-invariant, so that taking long differences between 2006 and 2010 removes it.

Conditional on the included regressors - the other quasi-fixed factors, the change in log sales, the changes in municipality-level relative wages, the three financial-crisis indicators, the 2006 relative gross profit margin, and region, industry and firm-age dummies - the change in the quasi-fixed factor of interest is uncorrelated with the differenced error of the share equation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing beyond the weighted correlations in Table 3; no balance table, pre-trend or placebo test is offered.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.
baseline_mean is null for the wage cost share models: Table 3 reports summary statistics for the employment-share dependent variables only.
The Low column is the derived fourth equation of the system, not a separately estimated regression: the four coefficients in each row sum to zero by construction.

evidence.how: Table 4 marks this coefficient with '**', and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p < 0.05.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

Table 3 reports means only for the employment-share dependent variables; the corresponding correlation and summary table for the wage cost share models is in the online supplementary material, so no mean of the change in wage cost shares is printed in the paper.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.
baseline_mean is null for the wage cost share models: Table 3 reports summary statistics for the employment-share dependent variables only.

evidence.how: Table 4 marks this coefficient with '*', and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p < 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

Table 3 reports means only for the employment-share dependent variables; the corresponding correlation and summary table for the wage cost share models is in the online supplementary material, so no mean of the change in wage cost shares is printed in the paper.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

outcome.label: Change in the firm's wage cost share of professionals and technicians, 2006-2010

register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: wage cost share (the firm's wage bill for the group divided by its total labour cost) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the professionals and technicians equation of the four-equation system.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point

estimand.target_population: Danish private-sector firms with at least 10 employees in both years that responded to both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys
estimand.time_horizon: change between 2006 and 2010 (a four-year long difference)
estimand.formal_query: gamma_{j,INV} in Eq. (6): the partial derivative of the expected change in the group's wage cost share with respect to the regressor, holding the other quasi-fixed factors, output, relative wages and the controls fixed. population.description: Danish private-sector firms present in both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA employer surveys (601 panel firms), excluding firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year, leaving 532 firms, linked to Danish register data on firms and working-age people
population.selection: DISKO4 produced 1775 employer responses and served as the sampling frame for GOPA, which produced 601 responses; DISKO4 oversampled firms from previous DISKO waves, so the panel is not representative of the Danish economy, and post-stratification weights for firm size and industry are used. Firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year are excluded because organizational practices require a minimum firm size to be meaningful.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-firm change between 2006 and 2010 in the quasi-fixed factors of the translog cost function - work organization (the DI and INV factors), an indicator of technological change in production, and the start or cessation of off-shoring - with firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity removed by long differencing. There is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument: the variation is the observed change in firms' own practices.

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity in the cost-minimization problem is additive and time-invariant, so that taking long differences between 2006 and 2010 removes it.

Conditional on the included regressors - the other quasi-fixed factors, the change in log sales, the changes in municipality-level relative wages, the three financial-crisis indicators, the 2006 relative gross profit margin, and region, industry and firm-age dummies - the change in the quasi-fixed factor of interest is uncorrelated with the differenced error of the share equation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing beyond the weighted correlations in Table 3; no balance table, pre-trend or placebo test is offered.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.
baseline_mean is null for the wage cost share models: Table 3 reports summary statistics for the employment-share dependent variables only.

evidence.how: Table 4 marks this coefficient with '***', and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p < 0.01.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

Table 3 reports means only for the employment-share dependent variables; the corresponding correlation and summary table for the wage cost share models is in the online supplementary material, so no mean of the change in wage cost shares is printed in the paper.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. baseline_mean is null for the wage cost share models: Table 3 reports summary statistics for the employment-share dependent variables only.

evidence.how: Table 4 marks this coefficient with '*', and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p < 0.1.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.
baseline_mean is null for the wage cost share models: Table 3 reports summary statistics for the employment-share dependent variables only.

evidence.how: Table 4 marks this coefficient with '***', and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p < 0.01.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

Table 3 reports means only for the employment-share dependent variables; the corresponding correlation and summary table for the wage cost share models is in the online supplementary material, so no mean of the change in wage cost shares is printed in the paper.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

definition.value: Binary variable coded 1 if the firm both prioritized technological change in production highly or very highly in its innovation effort and reports a great or some outcome from that effort. outcome.label: Change in the firm's wage cost share of middling-skill occupations, 2006-2010

register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: wage cost share (the firm's wage bill for the group divided by its total labour cost) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the middling-skill occupations (clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers) equation of the four-equation system.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.
baseline_mean is null for the wage cost share models: Table 3 reports summary statistics for the employment-share dependent variables only.

evidence.how: Table 4 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

Table 3 reports means only for the employment-share dependent variables; the corresponding correlation and summary table for the wage cost share models is in the online supplementary material, so no mean of the change in wage cost shares is printed in the paper.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

definition.value: Binary indicator that the firm has begun to off-shore between the two surveys. outcome.label: Change in the firm's wage cost share of professionals and technicians, 2006-2010

register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: wage cost share (the firm's wage bill for the group divided by its total labour cost) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the professionals and technicians equation of the four-equation system.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point

estimand.target_population: Danish private-sector firms with at least 10 employees in both years that responded to both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys
estimand.time_horizon: change between 2006 and 2010 (a four-year long difference)
estimand.formal_query: gamma_{j,AddOff} in Eq. (6): the partial derivative of the expected change in the group's wage cost share with respect to the regressor, holding the other quasi-fixed factors, output, relative wages and the controls fixed. population.description: Danish private-sector firms present in both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA employer surveys (601 panel firms), excluding firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year, leaving 532 firms, linked to Danish register data on firms and working-age people
population.selection: DISKO4 produced 1775 employer responses and served as the sampling frame for GOPA, which produced 601 responses; DISKO4 oversampled firms from previous DISKO waves, so the panel is not representative of the Danish economy, and post-stratification weights for firm size and industry are used. Firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year are excluded because organizational practices require a minimum firm size to be meaningful.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-firm change between 2006 and 2010 in the quasi-fixed factors of the translog cost function - work organization (the DI and INV factors), an indicator of technological change in production, and the start or cessation of off-shoring - with firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity removed by long differencing. There is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument: the variation is the observed change in firms' own practices.

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity in the cost-minimization problem is additive and time-invariant, so that taking long differences between 2006 and 2010 removes it.

Conditional on the included regressors - the other quasi-fixed factors, the change in log sales, the changes in municipality-level relative wages, the three financial-crisis indicators, the 2006 relative gross profit margin, and region, industry and firm-age dummies - the change in the quasi-fixed factor of interest is uncorrelated with the differenced error of the share equation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing beyond the weighted correlations in Table 3; no balance table, pre-trend or placebo test is offered.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.
baseline_mean is null for the wage cost share models: Table 3 reports summary statistics for the employment-share dependent variables only.

evidence.how: Table 4 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

Table 3 reports means only for the employment-share dependent variables; the corresponding correlation and summary table for the wage cost share models is in the online supplementary material, so no mean of the change in wage cost shares is printed in the paper.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. baseline_mean is null for the wage cost share models: Table 3 reports summary statistics for the employment-share dependent variables only.

evidence.how: Table 4 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-firm change between 2006 and 2010 in the quasi-fixed factors of the translog cost function - work organization (the DI and INV factors), an indicator of technological change in production, and the start or cessation of off-shoring - with firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity removed by long differencing. There is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument: the variation is the observed change in firms' own practices.

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity in the cost-minimization problem is additive and time-invariant, so that taking long differences between 2006 and 2010 removes it.

Conditional on the included regressors - the other quasi-fixed factors, the change in log sales, the changes in municipality-level relative wages, the three financial-crisis indicators, the 2006 relative gross profit margin, and region, industry and firm-age dummies - the change in the quasi-fixed factor of interest is uncorrelated with the differenced error of the share equation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing beyond the weighted correlations in Table 3; no balance table, pre-trend or placebo test is offered.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.
baseline_mean is null for the wage cost share models: Table 3 reports summary statistics for the employment-share dependent variables only.

evidence.how: Table 4 marks this coefficient with '*', and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p < 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

Table 3 reports means only for the employment-share dependent variables; the corresponding correlation and summary table for the wage cost share models is in the online supplementary material, so no mean of the change in wage cost shares is printed in the paper.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

outcome.label: Change in the firm's wage cost share of middling-skill occupations, 2006-2010

register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: wage cost share (the firm's wage bill for the group divided by its total labour cost) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the middling-skill occupations (clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers) equation of the four-equation system.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.

evidence.how: Table 5 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

claims.statement: DI (delegation and integration of functions) has no statistically significant association with the change in the firm's employment share of professionals and technicians between 2006 and 2010 (model 2, Table 5, column Profs/Techs).

treatment.label: DeltaDI - change 2006-2010 in the firm's score on the Delegation and Integration factor

definition.value: First factor of a principal components analysis of six organizational-practice questions (autonomous groups; systems for collecting proposals from employees; quality circles; delegation of responsibility; interdisciplinary workgroups; integration of functions), each a four-category variable (1 No/None, 2 Less than 25%, 3 25-50%, 4 over 50% of employees involved), asked identically in the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys and pooled over the resulting 1064 observations; the PCA uses weighted polychoric correlations and oblique rotation. The factor loads positively on autonomous teams, delegation of responsibility, interdisciplinary workgroups and integration of functions, and is labelled 'Delegation and Integration (DI)' in Table 2. The regressor is the firm's 2006-to-2010 long difference in this factor score; the paper notes that a unit change is very similar to a change of one standard deviation (Table 3 variance 1.156, mean of the change -0.110).

timing.value: Long difference between the 2006 DISKO4 survey and the 2010 GOPA survey, contemporaneous with the differenced outcome. The technology indicator refers to the innovation effort of 2007-2009 as reported in the 2010 survey, and the offshoring indicators to a change between the two survey years.

outcome.label: Change in the firm's employment share of professionals and technicians, 2006-2010

register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: employment share (the group's share of the firm's total employment) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the professionals and technicians equation of the four-equation system.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point

estimand.target_population: Danish private-sector firms with at least 10 employees in both years that responded to both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys
estimand.time_horizon: change between 2006 and 2010 (a four-year long difference)
estimand.formal_query: gamma_{j,DI} in Eq. (6): the partial derivative of the expected change in the group's employment share with respect to the regressor, holding the other quasi-fixed factors, output, relative wages and the controls fixed. The paper expresses it as a translog cost-function parameter, not in do-notation.

population.description: Danish private-sector firms present in both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA employer surveys (601 panel firms), excluding firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year, leaving 532 firms, linked to Danish register data on firms and working-age people
population.selection: DISKO4 produced 1775 employer responses and served as the sampling frame for GOPA, which produced 601 responses; DISKO4 oversampled firms from previous DISKO waves, so the panel is not representative of the Danish economy, and post-stratification weights for firm size and industry are used. Firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year are excluded because organizational practices require a minimum firm size to be meaningful.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-firm change between 2006 and 2010 in the quasi-fixed factors of the translog cost function - work organization (the DI and INV factors), an indicator of technological change in production, and the start or cessation of off-shoring - with firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity removed by long differencing. There is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument: the variation is the observed change in firms' own practices.

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity in the cost-minimization problem is additive and time-invariant, so that taking long differences between 2006 and 2010 removes it.

Conditional on the included regressors - the other quasi-fixed factors, the change in log sales, the changes in municipality-level relative wages, the three financial-crisis indicators, the 2006 relative gross profit margin, and region, industry and firm-age dummies - the change in the quasi-fixed factor of interest is uncorrelated with the differenced error of the share equation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing beyond the weighted correlations in Table 3; no balance table, pre-trend or placebo test is offered.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.

evidence.how: Table 5 marks this coefficient with '*', and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p < 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.
The Low column is the derived fourth equation of the system, not a separately estimated regression: the four coefficients in each row sum to zero by construction.

evidence.how: Table 5 marks this coefficient with '***', and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p < 0.01.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

definition.value: Second factor of the same principal components analysis; it captures employee involvement based on the use of quality circles and systems for collecting proposals from employees, and is labelled 'Involvement (INV)' in Table 2. register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: employment share (the group's share of the firm's total employment) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the managers equation of the four-equation system.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point

identification.source_of_variation: Within-firm change between 2006 and 2010 in the quasi-fixed factors of the translog cost function - work organization (the DI and INV factors), an indicator of technological change in production, and the start or cessation of off-shoring - with firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity removed by long differencing. There is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument: the variation is the observed change in firms' own practices.

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity in the cost-minimization problem is additive and time-invariant, so that taking long differences between 2006 and 2010 removes it.
