ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.
The Low column is the derived fourth equation of the system, not a separately estimated regression: the four coefficients in each row sum to zero by construction.

evidence.how: Table 6 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

definition.value: Interaction between the work-organization regressor and the moderator. Work-organization regressor: Second factor of the same principal components analysis; it captures employee involvement based on the use of quality circles and systems for collecting proposals from employees, and is labelled 'Involvement (INV)' in Table 2. The regressor is the firm's 2006-to-2010 long difference in this factor score; the paper notes that a unit change is very similar to a change of one standard deviation (Table 3 variance 1.179, mean of the change -0.115). The inter-factor correlation with DI is 0.529. Moderator (Started offshoring): Binary indicator that the firm has begun to off-shore between the two surveys. Both DISKO4 and GOPA ask about off-shoring but not identically, so only binary indicators of whether the firm uses off-shoring in each year can be constructed, from which 'started' and 'ceased' off-shoring are derived. Table 3 lists it as 'Add Offshoring' with mean 0.073; 7.3% of firms started offshoring. The coefficient is lambda in model 3, which adds 'interaction terms on the right hand side between the factors for work organization and the remaining quasi-fixed factors', sum_{m not in (Delta DI, Delta INV)} ( lambda_{j,m,DI} Delta DI_i + lambda_{j,m,INV} Delta INV_i ) ( Delta a_{m,i} ).

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.

evidence.how: Table 6 marks this coefficient with '***', and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p < 0.01.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

claims.statement: The interaction of INV (employee involvement) with Started offshoring has no statistically significant association with the change in the firm's employment share of professionals and technicians between 2006 and 2010 (model 3, Table 6, column Profs/Techs).

treatment.label: DeltaINV x Started offshoring (interaction term in model 3)

definition.value: Interaction between the work-organization regressor and the moderator. Work-organization regressor: Second factor of the same principal components analysis; it captures employee involvement based on the use of quality circles and systems for collecting proposals from employees, and is labelled 'Involvement (INV)' in Table 2. The regressor is the firm's 2006-to-2010 long difference in this factor score; the paper notes that a unit change is very similar to a change of one standard deviation (Table 3 variance 1.179, mean of the change -0.115). The inter-factor correlation with DI is 0.529. Moderator (Started offshoring): Binary indicator that the firm has begun to off-shore between the two surveys. Both DISKO4 and GOPA ask about off-shoring but not identically, so only binary indicators of whether the firm uses off-shoring in each year can be constructed, from which 'started' and 'ceased' off-shoring are derived. Table 3 lists it as 'Add Offshoring' with mean 0.073; 7.3% of firms started offshoring. The coefficient is lambda in model 3, which adds 'interaction terms on the right hand side between the factors for work organization and the remaining quasi-fixed factors', sum_{m not in (Delta DI, Delta INV)} ( lambda_{j,m,DI} Delta DI_i + lambda_{j,m,INV} Delta INV_i ) ( Delta a_{m,i} ).

timing.value: Long difference between the 2006 DISKO4 survey and the 2010 GOPA survey, contemporaneous with the differenced outcome. The technology indicator refers to the innovation effort of 2007-2009 as reported in the 2010 survey, and the offshoring indicators to a change between the two survey years.

outcome.label: Change in the firm's employment share of professionals and technicians, 2006-2010

register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: employment share (the group's share of the firm's total employment) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the professionals and technicians equation of the four-equation system.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point

estimand.target_population: Danish private-sector firms with at least 10 employees in both years that responded to both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys
estimand.time_horizon: change between 2006 and 2010 (a four-year long difference)
estimand.formal_query: lambda_{j,START,INV} in Eq. (6) with the model-3 interaction terms: the partial derivative of the expected change in the group's employment share with respect to the regressor, holding the other quasi-fixed factors, output, relative wages and the controls fixed. The paper expresses it as a translog cost-function parameter, not in do-notation.

population.description: Danish private-sector firms present in both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA employer surveys (601 panel firms), excluding firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year, leaving 532 firms, linked to Danish register data on firms and working-age people
population.selection: DISKO4 produced 1775 employer responses and served as the sampling frame for GOPA, which produced 601 responses; DISKO4 oversampled firms from previous DISKO waves, so the panel is not representative of the Danish economy, and post-stratification weights for firm size and industry are used. Firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year are excluded because organizational practices require a minimum firm size to be meaningful.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-firm change between 2006 and 2010 in the quasi-fixed factors of the translog cost function - work organization (the DI and INV factors), an indicator of technological change in production, and the start or cessation of off-shoring - with firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity removed by long differencing. There is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument: the variation is the observed change in firms' own practices.

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity in the cost-minimization problem is additive and time-invariant, so that taking long differences between 2006 and 2010 removes it.

Conditional on the included regressors - the other quasi-fixed factors, the change in log sales, the changes in municipality-level relative wages, the three financial-crisis indicators, the 2006 relative gross profit margin, and region, industry and firm-age dummies - the change in the quasi-fixed factor of interest is uncorrelated with the differenced error of the share equation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing beyond the weighted correlations in Table 3; no balance table, pre-trend or placebo test is offered.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.

evidence.how: Table 6 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.
The Low column is the derived fourth equation of the system, not a separately estimated regression: the four coefficients in each row sum to zero by construction.

evidence.how: Table 6 marks this coefficient with '*', and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p < 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

claims.statement: The interaction of INV (employee involvement) with Ceased offshoring has no statistically significant association with the change in the firm's employment share of managers between 2006 and 2010 (model 3, Table 6, column Mangers).

treatment.label: DeltaINV x Ceased offshoring (interaction term in model 3)

definition.value: Interaction between the work-organization regressor and the moderator. Work-organization regressor: Second factor of the same principal components analysis; it captures employee involvement based on the use of quality circles and systems for collecting proposals from employees, and is labelled 'Involvement (INV)' in Table 2. The regressor is the firm's 2006-to-2010 long difference in this factor score; the paper notes that a unit change is very similar to a change of one standard deviation (Table 3 variance 1.179, mean of the change -0.115). The inter-factor correlation with DI is 0.529. Moderator (Ceased offshoring): Binary indicator that the firm has ceased to off-shore between the two surveys, derived from the binary year-specific off-shoring indicators constructed from the non-identical DISKO4 and GOPA off-shoring questions. Table 3 lists it as 'Remove Offshoring' with mean 0.046; 4.6% of firms ceased offshoring. The coefficient is lambda in model 3, which adds 'interaction terms on the right hand side between the factors for work organization and the remaining quasi-fixed factors', sum_{m not in (Delta DI, Delta INV)} ( lambda_{j,m,DI} Delta DI_i + lambda_{j,m,INV} Delta INV_i ) ( Delta a_{m,i} ).

timing.value: Long difference between the 2006 DISKO4 survey and the 2010 GOPA survey, contemporaneous with the differenced outcome. The technology indicator refers to the innovation effort of 2007-2009 as reported in the 2010 survey, and the offshoring indicators to a change between the two survey years.

outcome.label: Change in the firm's employment share of managers, 2006-2010

register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: employment share (the group's share of the firm's total employment) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the managers equation of the four-equation system.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point

estimand.target_population: Danish private-sector firms with at least 10 employees in both years that responded to both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys
estimand.time_horizon: change between 2006 and 2010 (a four-year long difference)
estimand.formal_query: lambda_{j,CEASE,INV} in Eq. (6) with the model-3 interaction terms: the partial derivative of the expected change in the group's employment share with respect to the regressor, holding the other quasi-fixed factors, output, relative wages and the controls fixed. The paper expresses it as a translog cost-function parameter, not in do-notation.

population.description: Danish private-sector firms present in both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA employer surveys (601 panel firms), excluding firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year, leaving 532 firms, linked to Danish register data on firms and working-age people
population.selection: DISKO4 produced 1775 employer responses and served as the sampling frame for GOPA, which produced 601 responses; DISKO4 oversampled firms from previous DISKO waves, so the panel is not representative of the Danish economy, and post-stratification weights for firm size and industry are used. Firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year are excluded because organizational practices require a minimum firm size to be meaningful.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-firm change between 2006 and 2010 in the quasi-fixed factors of the translog cost function - work organization (the DI and INV factors), an indicator of technological change in production, and the start or cessation of off-shoring - with firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity removed by long differencing. There is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument: the variation is the observed change in firms' own practices.

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity in the cost-minimization problem is additive and time-invariant, so that taking long differences between 2006 and 2010 removes it.

Conditional on the included regressors - the other quasi-fixed factors, the change in log sales, the changes in municipality-level relative wages, the three financial-crisis indicators, the 2006 relative gross profit margin, and region, industry and firm-age dummies - the change in the quasi-fixed factor of interest is uncorrelated with the differenced error of the share equation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing beyond the weighted correlations in Table 3; no balance table, pre-trend or placebo test is offered.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.

evidence.how: Table 6 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.

evidence.how: Table 6 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

claims.statement: The interaction of INV (employee involvement) with Ceased offshoring has no statistically significant association with the change in the firm's employment share of low-skill occupations between 2006 and 2010 (model 3, Table 6, column Low).

treatment.label: DeltaINV x Ceased offshoring (interaction term in model 3)

definition.value: Interaction between the work-organization regressor and the moderator. Work-organization regressor: Second factor of the same principal components analysis; it captures employee involvement based on the use of quality circles and systems for collecting proposals from employees, and is labelled 'Involvement (INV)' in Table 2. The regressor is the firm's 2006-to-2010 long difference in this factor score; the paper notes that a unit change is very similar to a change of one standard deviation (Table 3 variance 1.179, mean of the change -0.115). The inter-factor correlation with DI is 0.529. Moderator (Ceased offshoring): Binary indicator that the firm has ceased to off-shore between the two surveys, derived from the binary year-specific off-shoring indicators constructed from the non-identical DISKO4 and GOPA off-shoring questions. Table 3 lists it as 'Remove Offshoring' with mean 0.046; 4.6% of firms ceased offshoring. The coefficient is lambda in model 3, which adds 'interaction terms on the right hand side between the factors for work organization and the remaining quasi-fixed factors', sum_{m not in (Delta DI, Delta INV)} ( lambda_{j,m,DI} Delta DI_i + lambda_{j,m,INV} Delta INV_i ) ( Delta a_{m,i} ).

timing.value: Long difference between the 2006 DISKO4 survey and the 2010 GOPA survey, contemporaneous with the differenced outcome. The technology indicator refers to the innovation effort of 2007-2009 as reported in the 2010 survey, and the offshoring indicators to a change between the two survey years.

outcome.label: Change in the firm's employment share of low-skill occupations, 2006-2010

register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: employment share (the group's share of the firm's total employment) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the low-skill occupations (service workers and shop and market sales workers, elementary occupations) equation of the four-equation system. The Low equation is not estimated directly: since the shares sum to unity it is sufficient to estimate J-1 = 3 equations and the fourth is derived from them, so the four coefficients in each row sum to zero.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point

estimand.target_population: Danish private-sector firms with at least 10 employees in both years that responded to both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys
estimand.time_horizon: change between 2006 and 2010 (a four-year long difference)
estimand.formal_query: lambda_{j,CEASE,INV} in Eq. (6) with the model-3 interaction terms: the partial derivative of the expected change in the group's employment share with respect to the regressor, holding the other quasi-fixed factors, output, relative wages and the controls fixed. The paper expresses it as a translog cost-function parameter, not in do-notation.

population.description: Danish private-sector firms present in both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA employer surveys (601 panel firms), excluding firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year, leaving 532 firms, linked to Danish register data on firms and working-age people
population.selection: DISKO4 produced 1775 employer responses and served as the sampling frame for GOPA, which produced 601 responses; DISKO4 oversampled firms from previous DISKO waves, so the panel is not representative of the Danish economy, and post-stratification weights for firm size and industry are used. Firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year are excluded because organizational practices require a minimum firm size to be meaningful.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-firm change between 2006 and 2010 in the quasi-fixed factors of the translog cost function - work organization (the DI and INV factors), an indicator of technological change in production, and the start or cessation of off-shoring - with firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity removed by long differencing. There is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument: the variation is the observed change in firms' own practices.

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity in the cost-minimization problem is additive and time-invariant, so that taking long differences between 2006 and 2010 removes it.

Conditional on the included regressors - the other quasi-fixed factors, the change in log sales, the changes in municipality-level relative wages, the three financial-crisis indicators, the 2006 relative gross profit margin, and region, industry and firm-age dummies - the change in the quasi-fixed factor of interest is uncorrelated with the differenced error of the share equation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing beyond the weighted correlations in Table 3; no balance table, pre-trend or placebo test is offered.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.

evidence.how: Table 6 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.

definition.value: First factor of a principal components analysis of six organizational-practice questions (autonomous groups; systems for collecting proposals from employees; quality circles; delegation of responsibility; interdisciplinary workgroups; integration of functions), each a four-category variable (1 No/None, 2 Less than 25%, 3 25-50%, 4 over 50% of employees involved), asked identically in the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys and pooled over the resulting 1064 observations; the PCA uses weighted polychoric correlations and oblique rotation. ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.
Table 7 prints no N, no R-squared and no number of imputations; those are carried from Table 6, the model 3 estimates the conditional marginal effects are computed from.
Table 7 reports a conditional marginal effect, i.e. the sum of the direct gamma and the relevant lambda from model 3, not a separate regression.

evidence.how: Table 7 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.
Table 7 prints no N. It reports conditional marginal effects computed from model 3, whose estimates are in Table 6 with N = 532 in all four columns.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

definition.value: First factor of a principal components analysis of six organizational-practice questions (autonomous groups; systems for collecting proposals from employees; quality circles; delegation of responsibility; interdisciplinary workgroups; integration of functions), each a four-category variable (1 No/None, 2 Less than 25%, 3 25-50%, 4 over 50% of employees involved), asked identically in the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys and pooled over the resulting 1064 observations; the PCA uses weighted polychoric correlations and oblique rotation. The factor loads positively on autonomous teams, delegation of responsibility, interdisciplinary workgroups and integration of functions, and is labelled 'Delegation and Integration (DI)' in Table 2. The regressor is the firm's 2006-to-2010 long difference in this factor score; the paper notes that a unit change is very similar to a change of one standard deviation (Table 3 variance 1.156, mean of the change -0.110). The reported number is the conditional marginal effect of this regressor in model 3, evaluated when technological change = 1: the direct effect plus the relevant interaction effect (Technological Change: Binary variable coded 1 if the firm both prioritized technological change in production highly or very highly in its innovation effort and reports a great or some outcome from that effort. Constructed from the 2010 GOPA survey, whose innovation questions refer to 2007-2009; priority is measured on a five-level Likert scale. 29% of firms had technical change over the period (Table 3 mean 0.289, where the variable is listed as 'DTechnology'). The paper has no direct indicator of qualitative change in capital equipment for 2006-2010; changes in the capital-labor ratio are used as an alternative measure in the online supplement.)

timing.value: Long difference between the 2006 DISKO4 survey and the 2010 GOPA survey, contemporaneous with the differenced outcome. ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.
Table 7 prints no N, no R-squared and no number of imputations; those are carried from Table 6, the model 3 estimates the conditional marginal effects are computed from.
Table 7 reports a conditional marginal effect, i.e. the sum of the direct gamma and the relevant lambda from model 3, not a separate regression.

evidence.how: Table 7 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.
Table 7 prints no N. It reports conditional marginal effects computed from model 3, whose estimates are in Table 6 with N = 532 in all four columns.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

definition.value: First factor of a principal components analysis of six organizational-practice questions (autonomous groups; systems for collecting proposals from employees; quality circles; delegation of responsibility; interdisciplinary workgroups; integration of functions), each a four-category variable (1 No/None, 2 Less than 25%, 3 25-50%, 4 over 50% of employees involved), asked identically in the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys and pooled over the resulting 1064 observations; the PCA uses weighted polychoric correlations and oblique rotation. The factor loads positively on autonomous teams, delegation of responsibility, interdisciplinary workgroups and integration of functions, and is labelled 'Delegation and Integration (DI)' in Table 2. The regressor is the firm's 2006-to-2010 long difference in this factor score; the paper notes that a unit change is very similar to a change of one standard deviation (Table 3 variance 1.156, mean of the change -0.110). The reported number is the conditional marginal effect of this regressor in model 3, evaluated when technological change = 1: the direct effect plus the relevant interaction effect (Technological Change: Binary variable coded 1 if the firm both prioritized technological change in production highly or very highly in its innovation effort and reports a great or some outcome from that effort. Constructed from the 2010 GOPA survey, whose innovation questions refer to 2007-2009; priority is measured on a five-level Likert scale. 29% of firms had technical change over the period (Table 3 mean 0.289, where the variable is listed as 'DTechnology'). The paper has no direct indicator of qualitative change in capital equipment for 2006-2010; changes in the capital-labor ratio are used as an alternative measure in the online supplement.)

timing.value: Long difference between the 2006 DISKO4 survey and the 2010 GOPA survey, contemporaneous with the differenced outcome. The technology indicator refers to the innovation effort of 2007-2009 as reported in the 2010 survey, and the offshoring indicators to a change between the two survey years.

outcome.label: Change in the firm's employment share of low-skill occupations, 2006-2010

register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: employment share (the group's share of the firm's total employment) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the low-skill occupations (service workers and shop and market sales workers, elementary occupations) equation of the four-equation system. The Low equation is not estimated directly: since the shares sum to unity it is sufficient to estimate J-1 = 3 equations and the fourth is derived from them, so the four coefficients in each row sum to zero.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point

estimand.target_population: Danish private-sector firms with at least 10 employees in both years that responded to both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys
estimand.time_horizon: change between 2006 and 2010 (a four-year long difference)
estimand.formal_query: gamma_{j,DI} + lambda_{j,TECH,DI} in Eq. (6) with the model-3 interaction terms: the partial derivative of the expected change in the group's employment share with respect to the regressor, holding the other quasi-fixed factors, output, relative wages and the controls fixed. The paper expresses it as a translog cost-function parameter, not in do-notation.

population.description: Danish private-sector firms present in both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA employer surveys (601 panel firms), excluding firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year, leaving 532 firms, linked to Danish register data on firms and working-age people
population.selection: DISKO4 produced 1775 employer responses and served as the sampling frame for GOPA, which produced 601 responses; DISKO4 oversampled firms from previous DISKO waves, so the panel is not representative of the Danish economy, and post-stratification weights for firm size and industry are used. Firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year are excluded because organizational practices require a minimum firm size to be meaningful.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-firm change between 2006 and 2010 in the quasi-fixed factors of the translog cost function - work organization (the DI and INV factors), an indicator of technological change in production, and the start or cessation of off-shoring - with firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity removed by long differencing. There is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument: the variation is the observed change in firms' own practices.

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity in the cost-minimization problem is additive and time-invariant, so that taking long differences between 2006 and 2010 removes it.

Conditional on the included regressors - the other quasi-fixed factors, the change in log sales, the changes in municipality-level relative wages, the three financial-crisis indicators, the 2006 relative gross profit margin, and region, industry and firm-age dummies - the change in the quasi-fixed factor of interest is uncorrelated with the differenced error of the share equation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing beyond the weighted correlations in Table 3; no balance table, pre-trend or placebo test is offered.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.
Table 7 prints no N, no R-squared and no number of imputations; those are carried from Table 6, the model 3 estimates the conditional marginal effects are computed from.
Table 7 reports a conditional marginal effect, i.e. the sum of the direct gamma and the relevant lambda from model 3, not a separate regression.

evidence.how: Table 7 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.
Table 7 prints no N. It reports conditional marginal effects computed from model 3, whose estimates are in Table 6 with N = 532 in all four columns.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.
Table 7 prints no N, no R-squared and no number of imputations; those are carried from Table 6, the model 3 estimates the conditional marginal effects are computed from.
Table 7 reports a conditional marginal effect, i.e. the sum of the direct gamma and the relevant lambda from model 3, not a separate regression.

evidence.how: Table 7 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.
Table 7 prints no N. It reports conditional marginal effects computed from model 3, whose estimates are in Table 6 with N = 532 in all four columns.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

claims.statement: DI (delegation and integration of functions) among firms that started offshoring has no statistically significant association with the change in the firm's employment share of middling-skill occupations between 2006 and 2010 (model 3 (conditional marginal effects), Table 7, column Middling).

treatment.label: DeltaDI marginal effect when started offshoring = 1 (conditional marginal effect from model 3)

definition.value: First factor of a principal components analysis of six organizational-practice questions (autonomous groups; systems for collecting proposals from employees; quality circles; delegation of responsibility; interdisciplinary workgroups; integration of functions), each a four-category variable (1 No/None, 2 Less than 25%, 3 25-50%, 4 over 50% of employees involved), asked identically in the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys and pooled over the resulting 1064 observations; the PCA uses weighted polychoric correlations and oblique rotation. The factor loads positively on autonomous teams, delegation of responsibility, interdisciplinary workgroups and integration of functions, and is labelled 'Delegation and Integration (DI)' in Table 2. The regressor is the firm's 2006-to-2010 long difference in this factor score; the paper notes that a unit change is very similar to a change of one standard deviation (Table 3 variance 1.156, mean of the change -0.110). The reported number is the conditional marginal effect of this regressor in model 3, evaluated when started offshoring = 1: the direct effect plus the relevant interaction effect (Started offshoring: Binary indicator that the firm has begun to off-shore between the two surveys. Both DISKO4 and GOPA ask about off-shoring but not identically, so only binary indicators of whether the firm uses off-shoring in each year can be constructed, from which 'started' and 'ceased' off-shoring are derived. Table 3 lists it as 'Add Offshoring' with mean 0.073; 7.3% of firms started offshoring.)

timing.value: Long difference between the 2006 DISKO4 survey and the 2010 GOPA survey, contemporaneous with the differenced outcome. The technology indicator refers to the innovation effort of 2007-2009 as reported in the 2010 survey, and the offshoring indicators to a change between the two survey years.

outcome.label: Change in the firm's employment share of middling-skill occupations, 2006-2010

register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: employment share (the group's share of the firm's total employment) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the middling-skill occupations (clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers) equation of the four-equation system.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point

estimand.target_population: Danish private-sector firms with at least 10 employees in both years that responded to both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys
estimand.time_horizon: change between 2006 and 2010 (a four-year long difference)
estimand.formal_query: gamma_{j,DI} + lambda_{j,START,DI} in Eq. (6) with the model-3 interaction terms: the partial derivative of the expected change in the group's employment share with respect to the regressor, holding the other quasi-fixed factors, output, relative wages and the controls fixed. The paper expresses it as a translog cost-function parameter, not in do-notation.

population.description: Danish private-sector firms present in both the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA employer surveys (601 panel firms), excluding firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year, leaving 532 firms, linked to Danish register data on firms and working-age people
population.selection: DISKO4 produced 1775 employer responses and served as the sampling frame for GOPA, which produced 601 responses; DISKO4 oversampled firms from previous DISKO waves, so the panel is not representative of the Danish economy, and post-stratification weights for firm size and industry are used. Firms with fewer than 10 employees in either year are excluded because organizational practices require a minimum firm size to be meaningful.

identification.source_of_variation: Within-firm change between 2006 and 2010 in the quasi-fixed factors of the translog cost function - work organization (the DI and INV factors), an indicator of technological change in production, and the start or cessation of off-shoring - with firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity removed by long differencing. There is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument: the variation is the observed change in firms' own practices.

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm-specific unobserved heterogeneity in the cost-minimization problem is additive and time-invariant, so that taking long differences between 2006 and 2010 removes it.

Conditional on the included regressors - the other quasi-fixed factors, the change in log sales, the changes in municipality-level relative wages, the three financial-crisis indicators, the 2006 relative gross profit margin, and region, industry and firm-age dummies - the change in the quasi-fixed factor of interest is uncorrelated with the differenced error of the share equation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing beyond the weighted correlations in Table 3; no balance table, pre-trend or placebo test is offered.

definition.value: employment share (the group's share of the firm's total employment) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.
Table 7 prints no N, no R-squared and no number of imputations; those are carried from Table 6, the model 3 estimates the conditional marginal effects are computed from.
Table 7 reports a conditional marginal effect, i.e. the sum of the direct gamma and the relevant lambda from model 3, not a separate regression.

evidence.how: Table 7 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.
Table 7 prints no N. It reports conditional marginal effects computed from model 3, whose estimates are in Table 6 with N = 532 in all four columns.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

ambiguities: The significance legend printed under Tables 4-7 reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.'; the third marker is clearly a typesetting error for '***', which is what the table bodies use. p_value is recorded from that legend as an inequality.

Statistical significance is coded from the printed stars, treating a single star (p < 0.1) as significant, which is how the paper itself reads the tables: it calls the unstarred Profs/Techs coefficient in Table 5 'not statistically significant' while describing starred coefficients as significant.

The paper words its findings as associations and as complementarity/substitutability in a production function ('are associated with', 'there is a positive relationship'), not as causal effects of an intervention. The design is a long-differenced firm-level regression with controls, not a quasi-experiment.

The paper also reports, in the same columns, the theta parameter on Delta ln(Sales), the beta parameters on the relative wages, and the eta parameters on the three financial-crisis variables and the 2006 relative gross profit margin. It states that the beta and theta parameters 'are not in focus in the current paper' and introduces the financial-crisis and profit-margin variables as controls, so no claim is recorded for them here.

baseline_mean is taken from the 'Mean' row of Table 3, which is the mean of the differenced dependent variable in the estimation sample, not a control-group or pre-period level: this design has no control group and the outcome is itself a change.
Table 7 prints no N, no R-squared and no number of imputations; those are carried from Table 6, the model 3 estimates the conditional marginal effects are computed from.
Table 7 reports a conditional marginal effect, i.e. the sum of the direct gamma and the relevant lambda from model 3, not a separate regression.

evidence.how: Table 7 marks this coefficient with no significance star, and the legend under the table reads '*p < 0.1, **: p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01.' (the third marker being a typographical error for '***'). Hence p >= 0.1.
No confidence interval is printed: Tables 4-7 report point estimates and robust standard errors only, with significance stars. No interval is derived from the standard error here.

No standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed. Table 3 reports the variance of the employment-share dependent variables (and splits it into within- and between-imputation variance), not a standard deviation; no conversion is made.

The share variables are fractions, not percentages: the text reads the Table 4 coefficient of -0.031 on DeltaINV for Middling as 'three percentage points', so a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point of the firm's wage cost (model 1) or employment (models 2 and 3) share.

The paper estimates long differences between the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys, so the regressor and the outcome are both changes accumulated over the same four years; horizon is recorded as 0 to 4 years, cumulative.
Table 7 prints no N. It reports conditional marginal effects computed from model 3, whose estimates are in Table 6 with N = 532 in all four columns.

The work-organization, technology and offshoring regressors come from the DISKO4 (2006) and GOPA (2010) employer surveys, not from a register; the paper names no register or register variable for them.

claims.statement: DI (delegation and integration of functions) among firms that ceased offshoring has no statistically significant association with the change in the firm's employment share of middling-skill occupations between 2006 and 2010 (model 3 (conditional marginal effects), Table 7, column Middling).

treatment.label: DeltaDI marginal effect when ceased offshoring = 1 (conditional marginal effect from model 3)

definition.value: First factor of a principal components analysis of six organizational-practice questions (autonomous groups; systems for collecting proposals from employees; quality circles; delegation of responsibility; interdisciplinary workgroups; integration of functions), each a four-category variable (1 No/None, 2 Less than 25%, 3 25-50%, 4 over 50% of employees involved), asked identically in the 2006 DISKO4 and the 2010 GOPA surveys and pooled over the resulting 1064 observations; the PCA uses weighted polychoric correlations and oblique rotation. The factor loads positively on autonomous teams, delegation of responsibility, interdisciplinary workgroups and integration of functions, and is labelled 'Delegation and Integration (DI)' in Table 2. The regressor is the firm's 2006-to-2010 long difference in this factor score; the paper notes that a unit change is very similar to a change of one standard deviation (Table 3 variance 1.156, mean of the change -0.110). The reported number is the conditional marginal effect of this regressor in model 3, evaluated when ceased offshoring = 1: the direct effect plus the relevant interaction effect (Ceased offshoring: Binary indicator that the firm has ceased to off-shore between the two surveys, derived from the binary year-specific off-shoring indicators constructed from the non-identical DISKO4 and GOPA off-shoring questions. Table 3 lists it as 'Remove Offshoring' with mean 0.046; 4.6% of firms ceased offshoring.)

timing.value: Long difference between the 2006 DISKO4 survey and the 2010 GOPA survey, contemporaneous with the differenced outcome. The technology indicator refers to the innovation effort of 2007-2009 as reported in the 2010 survey, and the offshoring indicators to a change between the two survey years.

register_source.value: Danish registry data on the populations of firms and working age people: each employment relation carries an occupation code and an hourly wage rate, aggregated to the firm. No register name or register variable code (e.g. an IDA or IND variable) is given.

definition.value: employment share (the group's share of the firm's total employment) for the occupation group, differenced between 2006 and 2010. Occupation groups follow the Goos et al. (2014) categorization of ISCO-88 1-digit major groups: managers; professionals and technicians/associate professionals (together with managers, 'high skill'); middling = clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers; low = service workers and shop and market sales workers, and elementary occupations. Shares are built from register data by aggregating all employment relations within the firm in 2006 and in 2010, each relation carrying an occupation code and an hourly wage rate; monetary values are deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index. This column is the middling-skill occupations (clerks, craft and related trades workers, plant and machine operators and assemblers) equation of the four-equation system.

timing.value: Change between 2006 and 2010, built from the register data for each of the two years.

units.value: change in the share (a fraction of the firm's total labour cost in model 1, of total employment in models 2 and 3) per one-unit change in the regressor; 0.01 = one percentage point
